purpose: Furosemide helps your body get rid of extra fluid that has built up, which can happen with conditions like heart failure, kidney disease, or liver problems. It reduces swelling in your legs, ankles, and feet, and can also help lower high blood pressure. Think of it as a medication that tells your kidneys to flush out extra water and salt through your urine.
how_it_works: Your kidneys normally filter your blood and decide what to keep and what to remove. Furosemide works by blocking a specific spot in your kidneys that would normally reabsorb salt and water back into your body. Because that salt and water can no longer be kept in, your body sends it out through your urine, which reduces the fluid buildup and swelling you feel.
common_side_effects: You will urinate much more often, especially in the first few hours after taking it. You may feel dizzy or lightheaded when you stand up quickly. Some people experience muscle cramps, thirst, or feel unusually tired. It can also lower important minerals in your blood like potassium, which is why your doctor may recommend eating bananas or taking a potassium supplement.
warnings: Do not take this medication if you are severely dehydrated or unable to urinate. Tell your doctor right away if you experience ringing in your ears, sudden hearing changes, severe dizziness, very little urination, or muscle weakness. If you are allergic to sulfa drugs, let your doctor know before starting this medication. Avoid standing up too fast as it can cause a sudden drop in blood pressure and make you faint. This medication may make your skin more sensitive to sunlight, so use sunscreen when outdoors.
typical_dosing: For most adults, the starting dose is usually 20 to 40 milligrams taken once a day in the morning. Your doctor may adjust your dose depending on how your body responds. It is best to take it in the morning so that the increased urination does not disturb your sleep at night. Always follow exactly what your doctor has prescribed for you.
